title: Steering committee Q&A rehearsal for consultants on Mac: a practical routine for 2026
metaTitle: Steering committee Q&A rehearsal for consultants on Mac
description: Rehearse steering committee Q&A on your Mac with a short routine, Keynote or PowerPoint cues, a question bank, and a live mock committee.
targetKeyword: steering committee Q&A rehearsal for consultants
intro: Steering committee Q&A rehearsal means practicing the hard questions before the meeting. You say the answers out loud, with your slides open. This page gives you a routine for a Mac, using tools you probably already have. It also covers where Lazur helps, and where it does not.
tldr: Build the question list from the committee members, not from your slides.
Rank each question by how much damage a weak answer would do.
Rehearse out loud with the slide on screen, in Keynote or PowerPoint, then run a live mock with a colleague.
Lazur answers questions about your screen out loud and drafts text. It does not play the committee.

blocks.text: Why steering committee questions are harder than a normal deck

A steering committee is a small group that decides whether your work continues, changes, or stops. Its members are usually senior and short on time. They rarely ask about the slide itself. They ask about the assumption behind it, and that is what you need to rehearse.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics says management analysts must convey information clearly in both writing and speaking. It lists making recommendations to management through presentations or written reports as a job task. A steering committee question is that task at its most exposed point.

BLS also says management analysts often work many hours under tight deadlines, and some work more than 40 hours per week. A tired presenter rehearses less. Put the rehearsal on the calendar before the deadline week fills up.

No study we could find measures how consultants prepare for client Q&A, or what weak answers cost in fees or trust. This page does not put a dollar figure on that. The steps below are practical habits, not a proven method.
Build the question list before you touch the deck

Most people start by rereading the slides. Start with the people instead. Write down each committee member, what they own, and what they would lose if the recommendation changed. Then write the questions each person is likely to ask first.

Pull questions from three places. The slides come first, since every number, claim, and recommendation is a target. The client's public material comes second, such as an annual report or published releases. The last meeting's notes come third. If someone pushed back then, expect the same push again.

blocks.caption: Question types to prepare, with what you need in hand.
rows: Where does this figure come from?
The source file, date, and owner of the figure
Why is this outside our brief?
The original brief and a plain line on the boundary
What happens if we wait a quarter?
The base case and the one assumption that drives it
Who wins and loses under this option?
A fair list of trade-offs for each group
How did you choose this sample?
The method in plain words and its limits

blocks.text: Write answers you can say out loud

A strong answer does three things. It answers the question in the first sentence. It gives one piece of evidence. It names the next step or the limit of what you know. Keep it short. Long answers invite the follow-up you were trying to avoid.
Write the answer the way you would say it, not the way a report reads. Then read it out loud. Replace any word that trips your tongue. In a Q&A room, rhythm matters more than polish.

Say 'I do not know' when you do not know. Then give the route to the answer, with a date. For example: 'I do not have the regional split with me. I will send it with the source by Friday.' Committees usually trust a named limit more than a confident guess.
Rehearse the slides in Keynote on Mac

If your deck is in Keynote, use the built-in rehearsal mode. Choose Play > Rehearse Slideshow. The presenter display opens without an external screen. Press X to switch between the presenter display and the slide. Press Esc to stop.

If a second display is connected, press ⌥X to choose which display you rehearse on. To edit notes, double-click the Presenter Notes field on the presenter display, then click Done. The Display Configuration button in the top-right corner lets you move or resize items.

blocks.title: Rehearsal mode does not ask questions
blocks.text: Keynote's rehearsal mode shows your slides and notes. It does not put questions to you. You still need a written list and a second person who will push.

Add a cue for each hard question to the presenter notes. Write the first sentence of the answer, and the slide where your evidence sits. When the question comes up in rehearsal, flip to that slide first. You practice the route, not only the words.
Rehearse delivery in PowerPoint with Speaker Coach

In PowerPoint for Mac, the feature is called Speaker Coach. Microsoft says it was previously known as Presenter Coach. Open the Slide Show tab, select Rehearse with Coach, and click Start Rehearsing. Speak when prompted. When you exit full screen, the Rehearsal Report opens.

Speaker Coach gives feedback on pacing, filler words, reading slide text, and similar delivery points. It needs a microphone and an internet connection. It only understands English, and it only runs when the Microsoft 365 interface language is English. Microsoft's support page says it is in free preview. Check what your own account shows.

Speaker Coach checks how you deliver the talk. It does not check whether your answer about the budget holds up. Microsoft's page does not say whether speaker notes or Presenter View work during a Speaker Coach rehearsal, so test that on your own machine first.

Use Speaker Coach on your opening and your first few minutes. Then switch to a live person for the content questions. If you still need to add notes first, the [guide to speaker notes in PowerPoint](/how-to/add-speaker-notes-in-powerpoint) walks through it.
Run a mock committee with a colleague

The strongest rehearsal is a live one. Ask a colleague who did not build the deck to play the committee. Give them your question list, but not your answers. Ask them to pick the question they dislike most and push on it.

Set up the room the way the real meeting will run. Put the slide on screen. Let them interrupt. If the committee meets on a video call, run the mock on Zoom with the same screen share, so you practice the setup you will actually use.

Judge each answer on three checks. Did the answer come in the first sentence? Did it include evidence? Did it name a next step or a limit? Change an answer only where a check failed. Rewriting everything after every session wastes time.
If no colleague is free, record yourself on your phone, answering each question out loud. Listen back for filler words and for the spot where you started to read.
Mistakes that make Q&A rehearsal useless

items: Reading answers from the notes word for word. You sound scripted the moment the question changes.
Rehearsing only the easy questions. The damage sits in the question you hoped they would skip.
Practicing alone and calling it finished. A quiet room hides the filler words you use under pressure.
Repeating the deck in your answer. The committee has already read the slides.
Changing the answer after every session. Pick one version, then test it at least once more before the meeting.
Pasting client figures into a tool before checking your firm's rules on confidential data.

blocks.text: Handle the questions you did not predict

Some questions will not be on your list. Prepare a bridge. Try: 'That is a fair challenge. Here is what I can answer now, and here is what I will check.' Then answer the part you know. A bridge keeps you talking while you think.
Watch for questions that test the team, not the work. A question like 'Who signed off on this?' is often about accountability. Answer the fact first. Do not argue about the person asking.

Keep a one-page sheet of hard facts. For each key figure, list the source, the date, and the owner. Keep that numbers sheet in Excel, so you can check a figure in seconds. A fast, accurate source beats a clever answer in a live room.
Where Lazur helps, and where it does not

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥⌘ to ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud, and it can point at things. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it on your screen.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. That helps when you draft a first version of an answer. Ask Lazur to guide you through a menu, and it walks you one click at a time, waiting for each click. You still do the clicking.
Lazur does not play the committee. It does not push back on your answers or score them. Treat it as a helper for the prep, the notes, and the follow-up, not as the room.

blocks.title: Check client data first
blocks.text: Check your firm's rules before you paste slides, notes, or client figures into any AI tool. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer, and says they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Your firm's policy still decides what you may share.
Edge cases to plan for before the meeting

If the committee includes people from outside your firm, learn about them from public material only. Read the client's website, annual report, or published releases. Do not dig through personal profiles to find pressure points. That reads badly when it surfaces in the room.

If the work is client-confidential, rehearse with placeholders. Replace names and exact figures with labels while you practice. Put the real values back in the room, from the approved file your firm uses.

If the committee is about to reject your recommendation, rehearse that too. Practice saying what you recommend, what evidence would change your view, and how you will support the decision if it goes the other way. Committees remember who handled a no well.
What to do after the meeting

Write down every question you got, in the committee's own words. Sort each one into the question types from the table. Add the new ones to your question bank. The next committee will ask a version of them.
Send any follow-ups within the time you promised. Draft the note in Outlook, then read it out loud once before you send it. Late follow-ups weaken a strong answer.
Use the plan below as a starting point. Move the days to fit the meeting date, and keep the final day as a fixed block on your calendar.

faq.question: What is steering committee Q&A rehearsal?
faq.answer: It is practice answering the hard questions a steering committee might ask, out loud, before the meeting. You build a list of likely questions, write short answers, and rehearse with the slides open or with a colleague playing the committee.

faq.question: How do I rehearse slides in Keynote on Mac?
faq.answer: Choose Play > Rehearse Slideshow. Press X to switch between the presenter display and the slide, and Esc to stop. Add a cue for each hard question in the presenter notes so you practice the route to the right slide.

faq.question: Does Speaker Coach help with tough questions?
faq.answer: Speaker Coach gives feedback on delivery, such as pacing and filler words. It works in English only and needs a microphone and an internet connection. It does not judge the content of your answers, so pair it with a live colleague.

faq.question: Can Lazur play the steering committee?
faq.answer: No. Lazur answers questions about your screen out loud, points at things, guides you one click at a time, dictates text, and drafts text. It does not play the client or score your answers.

faq.question: How long should a rehearsal session run?
faq.answer: Keep each session short enough that you stay sharp to the end. Stop when your answers stop improving, not when the clock says so.

faq.question: Can I paste client figures into an AI tool?
faq.answer: Check your firm's rules first, since they come before any tool. Lazur sends audio and the screenshot to AI providers to answer, and says they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.

faq.question: What if I do not know the answer in the room?
faq.answer: Say so, then give the route to the answer and a date. Committees usually respond better to a clear limit than to a guess that breaks under a follow-up.

faq.question: Who should play the committee in a mock?
faq.answer: Someone who did not build the deck and will push. A peer from another team works well. Give them the question list, but keep your answers to yourself.

costs.title: Credibility in the room
costs.text: A question you cannot answer changes how the room sees the whole deck. The slide that looked settled now looks untested. Recovering takes more of the meeting than a clean answer would have. Committee members remember the moment, not the chart.

costs.title: Late nights before the deadline
costs.text: BLS says management analysts often work many hours under tight deadlines, and some work more than 40 hours per week. Without a rehearsal routine, the Q&A gets built at night. That is when you have the least energy to think clearly.

costs.title: A recommendation that stalls
costs.text: If a weak answer makes the committee doubt the analysis, the decision can wait for another meeting. That delay can cost the client more than the answer did. No study we found measures this for consultants, so treat it as a risk, not a number.

costs.title: Nerves that carry over
costs.text: A meta-analysis of 62 psychological interventions for fear of public speaking found a pooled effect of g = 0.74 across 30 trials. It studied public speaking in general, not consultants or client Q&A. It did not isolate rehearsal or skills training, so it cannot say which part helped.

costs.title: Burnout on top of deadlines
costs.text: Gallup reports that 27% of US full-time employees very often or always feel burned out at work in Q2 2026. Gallup does not connect that figure to committee questions. Still, a dreaded Q&A adds stress to a schedule that is already full.

causes.title: The deck is built to be read, not questioned
causes.text: Slides are written to carry a story. Committee members read them in advance and look for the gap in the logic. The question often sits between two slides, where nobody wrote the answer down.

causes.title: You rehearse the talk, not the challenge
causes.text: Most teams run the presentation from start to finish and call it prepared. That practice covers the opening well. The hard questions come at the end, when the room is tired and your energy is low.

causes.title: No one on the team plays the committee
causes.text: Your team knows the project too well. They fill gaps without noticing. A committee member does not share your assumptions, so they ask about the assumption you skipped.

causes.title: Deadlines push prep to the last day
causes.text: BLS describes management analysts as often working many hours under tight deadlines. When the deadline is the meeting, the Q&A is the first thing cut. That is how weak answers end up in the room.

causes.title: The committee changes faster than your notes
causes.text: Steering committees change membership and priorities. A question that did not matter last quarter can matter now. If you do not track what the committee cares about, you guess at the risk.

causes.title: Stress makes answers come out wrong
causes.text: WHO describes burn-out as a syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. A stressed presenter loses the thread faster under pressure. That is a reason to rehearse early, not the night before.

fixes.title: Build the list from the committee members
fixes.text: For each member, write what they own and what they risk losing. Then write the questions each one would ask first. Use the last meeting's notes and any written pushback you have on file.

fixes.title: Rank questions by damage, not by likelihood
fixes.text: Put each question on a simple scale of how much a weak answer would hurt the recommendation. The questions with the highest damage get the first and longest rehearsal, even if they are unlikely.

fixes.title: Write each answer in speaking order
fixes.text: Open with the direct answer. Add the evidence. End with the next step or the honest limit. Write it as speech, read it out loud, and cut any word you would not say in the room.

fixes.title: Rehearse with the right slide open
fixes.text: In Keynote, use Play > Rehearse Slideshow and keep the cue for each hard question in the presenter notes. Practice flipping to the slide, answering, and returning to the flow of the talk.

fixes.title: Run a cold read with a colleague's worst questions
fixes.text: Ask a colleague for the most annoying questions they can think of. Answer them with no notes and no pause to prepare. Keep the answers that land, and rewrite the ones that wander.

fixes.title: Use Speaker Coach for delivery, then go live
fixes.text: In PowerPoint for Mac, open the Slide Show tab, select Rehearse with Coach, and click Start Rehearsing. Read the Rehearsal Report for pacing and filler words. Then move to a live person for the content questions.

fixes.title: State the limit before someone else does
fixes.text: Write down what the data does not show, and say it in the room before anyone asks. A committee trusts a named limit more than a confident guess that breaks under one follow-up.

fixes.title: Put the rehearsal on the calendar
fixes.text: Book the rehearsal the same way you book the meeting. Treat it as a fixed block. If the deadline moves, keep the block and shorten the deck instead of cutting the practice.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Build the committee map
plan.text: Write each committee member, what they own, and what they risk losing. Add the questions each person is likely to ask. Pull them from the deck, the client's public material, and the last meeting's notes.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Rank and draft the answers
plan.text: Rank every question by how much a weak answer would hurt. Draft a short answer for the risky ones, in speaking order: direct answer, evidence, then the next step or the limit.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Cue the slides
plan.text: In Keynote, use Play > Rehearse Slideshow and add a cue to the presenter notes for each hard question. In PowerPoint, add speaker notes and check that the slide for each answer is easy to reach.

plan.label: Day 4
plan.title: Cold reads out loud
plan.text: Read each answer out loud, once, with no notes. Cut any word you would not say. Keep the session short enough that you stay sharp, and stop when the answers stop improving.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Live mock committee
plan.text: Ask a colleague who did not build the deck to play the committee. Give them the question list only. Note each place you stalled, and rewrite only those answers.

plan.label: Day 6
plan.title: Delivery check
plan.text: Run Speaker Coach in PowerPoint for Mac through Slide Show > Rehearse with Coach. Fix pacing and filler words in your opening. Keep the content answers from your live mock, not from the coach.

plan.label: Day 7
plan.title: Final pass and sources
plan.text: Check each figure against its source, and mark any number you cannot source as a limit to say out loud. Paste no client data into a tool until your firm's rules allow it. Save the question bank for the next meeting.
